# Health-Journal Prose — Real Example Sentences

Concrete companion to `health_journal_prose_style.md`. That file states the
conventions; this file **shows them**, using short sentences quoted from
published articles in the target journals so the English has a real model to
imitate.

**How to use these.** Imitate the **structure and register** — sentence shape,
where the number sits, how the hedge names its reason, how the contrast turns —
**never the content or wording**. These are other authors' sentences about other
studies; lifting a phrase into a new manuscript is plagiarism. Write your own
sentence about your own result in the same shape.

**Attribution & scope.** Each quotation is brief (one sentence), cited to its
journal and DOI, and reproduced here for the purpose of style illustration
(fair-use commentary). Minor OCR artefacts in the source have been cleaned.
Coverage is a curated sample of JAMA, BMJ, *Lancet Digital Health*, *Nature* /
*Nature Medicine* / *npj Digital Medicine* and *World Psychiatry* articles from
the reference corpus — not an exhaustive set.

---

## 1. Titles — population/object + design after a colon

- *"Evaluation of symptom checkers for self diagnosis and triage: audit study."*
  — BMJ (doi:10.1136/bmj.h3480)
- *"Charting the evolution of artificial intelligence mental health chatbots from
  rule-based systems to large language models: a systematic review."*
  — World Psychiatry (doi:10.1002/wps.21352)
- *"Accuracy of online symptom assessment applications, large language models,
  and laypeople for self-triage decisions."* — npj Digital Medicine
  (doi:10.1038/s41746-025-01566-6)

**Why they work:** each names the *object of study* and the *design*, states no
finding, and is not a question or a slogan. The colon carries the design label.

---

## 2. Results — lead with the pattern, numbers with denominators and CIs

- *"Performance on appropriate triage advice across the 23 individual symptom
  checkers ranged from 33% (95% confidence interval 19% to 48%) to 78% (64% to
  91%) of standardized patient evaluations."* — BMJ (doi:10.1136/bmj.h3480)
- *"The average accuracy of large language models ranged from 57.8% to 70.0%."*
  — npj Digital Medicine (doi:10.1038/s41746-025-01566-6)

**Why they work:** the estimate travels with its 95% CI in the same parentheses;
the range is anchored to a stated denominator noun ("standardized patient
evaluations"); no interpretation intrudes into the number. (Note the **BMJ CI
style** — "19% to 48%"; JAMA uses "19%-48%" with a comma. Pick one per paper.)

---

## 3. The contrastive turn — `However,` doing the work

- *"However, the generated output depends greatly on the initial input."*
  — JAMA Network Open (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.57879)
- *"However, self-consistency led to a drop in performance for the PubMedQA
  dataset."* — Nature (doi:10.1038/s41586-023-06291-2)
- *"However, these models also pose a danger of perpetuating biases and
  delivering incorrect medical diagnoses, which can have a direct, harmful
  impact on medical care."* — Lancet Digital Health
  (doi:10.1016/S2589-7500(23)00225-X)

**Why they work:** one clean pivot on a genuine contrast; no stacking of
`Nevertheless` / `Conversely` / `Importantly`. The short factual contrasts
(first two) sit next to a longer consequence-bearing one — rhythm by design.

---

## 4. Hedging that names its specific reason

- *"Second, the exclusion of multimodal tasks and basic biological science
  research might have led to an incomplete picture of large language model
  applications in health care."* — JAMA (doi:10.1001/jama.2024.21700)
- *"Although this improvement may seem small, the single-rater human performance
  on PubMedQA is 78.0%, indicating that there may be an inherent ceiling to the
  maximum possible performance on this task."* — Nature
  (doi:10.1038/s41586-023-06291-2)
- *"However, we believe similar biases might be present more broadly within other
  large language models, all of which warrant caution before deployment in a
  health-care setting."* — Lancet Digital Health
  (doi:10.1016/S2589-7500(23)00225-X)

**Why they work:** the hedge (`might`, `may`) is attached to the *specific
feature of this study* that creates the uncertainty — an excluded task type, a
known human ceiling, a scope of generalisation — not a free-floating "results
should be interpreted with caution".

---

## 5. The gap statement — motivating the study

- *"However, there is no evidence synthesis on the accuracy of large language
  models, and no review has contextualized the accuracy of symptom-assessment
  apps and large language models."* — npj Digital Medicine
  (doi:10.1038/s41746-025-01566-6)
- *"However, compared with non-AI tools, the highly complicated underlying data
  processing frequently comes with a lack of transparency into the exact working
  mechanisms."* — BMJ (doi:10.1136/bmj-2024-081554)

**Why they work:** the gap is stated as a specific absence ("no review has
contextualized…"), which the study then fills — not a vague "little is known".

---

## 6. Limitations — named, with what they affect

- *"Our investigation identified a limitation in the ability of GPT-4 to generate
  clinical cases that captured the true demographic diversity of medical
  conditions."* — Lancet Digital Health (doi:10.1016/S2589-7500(23)00225-X)
- *"Another limitation concerns the unequal number of studies included for
  symptom-assessment apps, large language models, and laypeople,
  respectively."* — npj Digital Medicine (doi:10.1038/s41746-025-01566-6)

**Why they work:** each names a *specific* limitation and what it bears on, and
the enumerator ("Another…", and JAMA's "Second,…" in §4) marks the standard
`First, / Second, / Third,` limitations shape. Neither closes with a generic
reassurance.

---

## 7. Conclusions — restate design + n, at the strength the results carry

- *"In this systematic review of 137 chatbot health advice studies, the reporting
  quality was heterogeneous and may inform the development of the CHART reporting
  standards."* — JAMA Network Open (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.57879)
- *"To the best of our knowledge, no study has systematically evaluated the impact
  of biases in GPT-4 for clinical applications."* — Lancet Digital Health
  (doi:10.1016/S2589-7500(23)00225-X)

**Why they work:** the Conclusions sentence opens by naming the **design and the
sample size** ("In this systematic review of 137 …"), then states what follows at
a measured strength (`may inform`). Novelty is **bounded** ("to the best of our
knowledge"), never a bare "this is the first".

---

## 8. Putting it together — a short worked contrast

Weak (generic, could be any paper):

> "Our comprehensive analysis revealed that chatbots showed promising but
> concerning results, and it is important to note that further research is
> needed in this crucial area."

Rewritten in the corpus register (your own numbers, your own study):

> "Across the 12 studies, triage accuracy ranged from 41% to 88% (see Table 2).
> Accuracy was lower for emergency presentations, however, where under-triage
> could delay care. Because every study used vignettes rather than real patients,
> these estimates may not transfer to live use."

**What changed:** the vague intensifiers ("comprehensive", "promising but
concerning", "crucial", "further research is needed") are gone; the finding
leads with a number and denominator; the contrast turns once on `however`; and
the hedge names the specific reason (vignettes, not real patients).

---

**Epistemic status:** brief attributed quotations reproduced for style
illustration. They model English *structure*, not content — write your own
sentence about your own study. Where a target journal's author instructions
differ, the journal governs; the claim-strength ladder and protected hedges
still apply (a style edit never moves a claim's strength).
